narrative:
The model estimated a 12% chance that you will fail your final year—roughly a one-in-eight risk. Although that is a relatively low probability, the decision still places you in the group required to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The explanation is somewhat reassuring: the three strongest influences on the prediction all worked toward passing, not failing. The most influential was your reason for choosing the school. You selected it for its reputation; among students who passed, reputation was a common reason, and this counted in your favor. The second strongest was your record of past failures: you have none, matching the average for students who passed, which lowers concern. Third was the quality of your family relationships, rated good; most students who passed also reported good relationships, so this is another protective factor. The overall failing flag therefore looks precautionary rather than strongly driven by these top factors, which is consistent with the low 12% figure.

What should you consider next? Use the remedial support to protect against the remaining risk. Your attendance is the clearest practical concern: 10 absences is well above the average of about 3.8 among students who passed. Also, your free time is very high and going out is high compared with most passers, so build a steadier study routine. Since you receive family support, want higher education, and have home internet, use those strengths to keep up with coursework and attend consistently.
